projects.name: Shipment tracking migration from MongoDB to PostgreSQL
projects.summary: Moved the shipment tracking history store from MongoDB to PostgreSQL with zero downtime using dual writes, a throttled backfill and a feature-flagged read switch.
projects.problem: Tracking history lived in MongoDB while the rest of the shipment data was in PostgreSQL. Cross-store queries were done in application code, which made the tracking timeline endpoint slow and made reporting queries impossible to write in SQL.
projects.context: Tracking events arrive from many carriers with different payload shapes. The tracking timeline is one of the most used customer-facing endpoints, so downtime was not acceptable.
objectives: Store tracking events in PostgreSQL next to shipments.
Migrate existing history without downtime or data loss.
my_contributions: Designed the new tracking_events table, including a JSONB column for carrier-specific payloads.
Implemented the dual-write layer so new events were written to both MongoDB and PostgreSQL.
Wrote the batched backfill job with validation and a quarantine table for malformed documents.
Switched reads to PostgreSQL behind a feature flag and led the cutover.
Removed the MongoDB write path after the verification period.
projects.implementation: Python service using SQLAlchemy models and Alembic migrations. New events were written to both stores through a repository class that hid the dual write from callers. The backfill read MongoDB in batches ordered by _id, validated and normalised each document, and inserted with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING so it could be safely re-run. A feature flag switched the timeline endpoint to read from PostgreSQL per tenant, which allowed a gradual rollout.
projects.architecture: Shipments API (FastAPI) -> TrackingRepository -> PostgreSQL (primary) with temporary dual write to MongoDB. Backfill runs as a separate one-off job. Reads are routed by a per-tenant feature flag during rollout.

challenges.challenge: Older MongoDB documents were inconsistent: missing fields, mixed timestamp formats and duplicated events.
challenges.solution: Added a validation step in the backfill that normalised timestamps to UTC, de-duplicated by (shipment_id, carrier_event_id), and moved unfixable documents to a quarantine table for manual review.

challenges.challenge: Running the backfill against the production database risked slowing down live traffic.
challenges.solution: Processed data in batches of 5,000 with keyset pagination and a configurable sleep between batches, and ran it outside peak hours.

decisions.context: The migration had to happen without downtime on a heavily used endpoint.
decisions.decision: Use dual writes, then backfill, then switch reads behind a per-tenant feature flag.
decisions.reasoning: Each step could be verified and rolled back independently, and rollout could start with low-traffic tenants.
alternatives: Big-bang migration in a maintenance window
decisions.tradeoffs: Temporary extra write latency and code complexity while both stores were kept in sync.

decisions.context: Each carrier sends tracking events with different extra fields.
decisions.decision: Store common fields as typed columns and carrier-specific data in a JSONB column.
decisions.reasoning: Keeps the common query paths indexed and typed without needing a table per carrier.
decisions.tradeoffs: Carrier-specific fields are harder to query and validate at the database level.

projects.name: Reliable webhook delivery with retries
projects.summary: Rebuilt outbound customer webhooks on a PostgreSQL-backed job queue with exponential backoff, a dead-letter table and idempotency keys.
projects.problem: Webhooks were sent inline during request handling. If a customer endpoint was slow or down, the event was lost and the original request became slow.
projects.context: Customers rely on webhooks to update their own systems when a shipment status changes. Roughly 50,000 webhooks were sent per day.
objectives: Stop losing webhooks when customer endpoints fail.
Remove webhook sending from the request path.
Give customers a way to detect duplicate deliveries.
my_contributions: Proposed and implemented the PostgreSQL-backed delivery queue using an outbox table.
Implemented the retry worker with exponential backoff and jitter.
Added the dead-letter table and an internal endpoint to replay failed deliveries.
Added idempotency keys to webhook payloads and documented them for customers.
Wrote unit and integration tests for retry scheduling and worker concurrency.
projects.implementation: The request handler inserts a delivery row into an outbox table in the same transaction as the status change. Worker processes claim rows using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, send the HTTP request with a timeout, and on failure reschedule with exponential backoff and jitter (up to 8 attempts over about 24 hours). After the final attempt the row moves to a dead-letter table. Each payload carries an Idempotency-Key header derived from the event ID.
projects.architecture: Shipments API writes to an outbox table -> worker processes in notifications-service poll and claim jobs with SKIP LOCKED -> customer endpoints. Failed jobs go to a dead-letter table that can be replayed through an internal API.

challenges.challenge: Multiple workers could pick up the same job and send duplicate webhooks.
challenges.solution: Used FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED to claim jobs atomically, and added idempotency keys so customers can safely ignore any remaining duplicates.

challenges.challenge: A single customer endpoint that was down generated a large number of retries.
challenges.solution: Capped attempts and added jitter so retries were spread out instead of arriving in bursts.

decisions.context: Needed a durable queue for webhook jobs.
decisions.decision: Use a PostgreSQL table with SKIP LOCKED instead of introducing a message broker.
decisions.reasoning: About 50,000 jobs per day is well within what PostgreSQL can handle, the team already operated PostgreSQL, and the outbox pattern gives transactional enqueueing for free.
decisions.tradeoffs: Polling adds some database load and the throughput ceiling is lower than a dedicated broker.

decisions.context: Needed a retry policy that recovers from short outages without overloading customers.
decisions.decision: Exponential backoff with full jitter, maximum 8 attempts, then dead-letter.
decisions.reasoning: Covers outages of up to about a day while avoiding synchronised retry bursts.

metrics.name: Webhooks permanently failed after all retries

projects.name: Carrier rate aggregation service
projects.summary: Node.js/TypeScript service that fetches shipping rates from several carrier APIs in parallel and returns them in one normalised format. Built together with another engineer.
projects.problem: The checkout flow called each carrier API one after another, so quoting was slow and every carrier returned a different response format.
objectives: Return quotes from all carriers in one response.
Keep checkout fast even if one carrier is slow.
Use a single normalised rate format.
my_contributions: Implemented the adapters for two of the five carriers.
Wrote the normalisation layer that converts units and currencies into one rate format.
Added per-carrier timeouts so slow carriers return partial results instead of blocking the response.
Added contract tests based on recorded carrier responses.
projects.implementation: Each carrier has an adapter implementing a common interface (getRates). The service calls all adapters in parallel using Promise.allSettled with a per-carrier timeout and returns whatever succeeded, marking the rest as unavailable. Responses pass through a normalisation step that converts weight units and currencies. An existing Redis cache, set up by a teammate, stores quotes for a short time.

challenges.challenge: Carriers returned different units, currencies and field names.
challenges.solution: Created a single normalised rate type and per-carrier mapping functions, with tests for each mapping.

challenges.challenge: One carrier's sandbox API was unreliable, which made tests flaky.
challenges.solution: Recorded real sandbox responses as fixtures and used them in contract tests.

decisions.context: A slow carrier could delay the whole checkout quote.
decisions.decision: Call carriers in parallel with a per-carrier timeout and return partial results.
decisions.reasoning: Checkout speed mattered more than always showing every carrier.
decisions.tradeoffs: Customers sometimes see fewer carrier options when a carrier is slow.

projects.name: Shipment search endpoint performance
projects.summary: Made the shipment search API several times faster by fixing an N+1 query problem, adding targeted indexes and switching to keyset pagination.
projects.problem: The shipment search endpoint became slow for large tenants, with p95 latency over 2 seconds and timeouts on later pages.
objectives: Bring p95 search latency under 500 ms.
my_contributions: Profiled the endpoint and found an N+1 query caused by lazy-loaded relationships.
Replaced lazy loading with selectinload for the relationships used by the endpoint.
Added a composite index on (tenant_id, created_at) and a trigram index for reference number search.
Replaced offset pagination with keyset (cursor) pagination.
projects.implementation: Used SQL query logging and EXPLAIN ANALYZE to find slow queries. Changed the SQLAlchemy query to use selectinload, reducing 52 queries per request to 3. Added a composite B-tree index matching the default sort and a GIN pg_trgm index for partial reference number search. Replaced OFFSET with a cursor based on (created_at, id).

challenges.challenge: Deep pages became slower and slower with OFFSET pagination.
challenges.solution: Switched to keyset pagination so every page costs about the same.

decisions.context: Users needed partial matching on reference numbers.
decisions.decision: Use PostgreSQL pg_trgm with a GIN index instead of adding a search engine.
decisions.reasoning: Met the requirement without operating new infrastructure.
decisions.tradeoffs: Less flexible ranking and text search features than a dedicated search engine.

decisions.context: Offset pagination was slow for deep pages.
decisions.decision: Use keyset pagination with an opaque cursor.
decisions.reasoning: Consistent performance regardless of page depth and stable results when new rows arrive.
alternatives: Keep OFFSET and cap the maximum page number
decisions.tradeoffs: Clients can no longer jump directly to an arbitrary page number.

projects.name: Support documentation assistant (prototype)
projects.summary: Prototype RAG assistant that answers internal support questions from help-centre articles, with citations to source articles.
projects.problem: Support agents spent a lot of time searching help-centre articles to answer repeated customer questions.
objectives: Answer support questions using only internal documentation.
Show which articles each answer is based on.
my_contributions: Built the ingestion script that splits articles by heading and stores embeddings in pgvector.
Implemented retrieval and a prompt that requires the model to cite article IDs.
Tried a cross-encoder reranking step in a separate PR that was not merged.
projects.implementation: Python scripts chunk help-centre articles by section heading, generate embeddings and store them in PostgreSQL with pgvector. At query time the top 5 chunks by cosine similarity are added to a prompt that instructs the LLM to answer only from the given chunks and cite their article IDs.

challenges.challenge: The model sometimes answered from general knowledge when the articles did not cover the question.
challenges.solution: Changed the prompt to require citations and to reply that the documentation does not cover the question when no chunk is relevant.

decisions.context: Needed somewhere to store embeddings for the prototype.
decisions.decision: Use pgvector in the existing PostgreSQL instance.
decisions.reasoning: Avoided adding a separate vector database for a prototype.

projects.name: Structured logging and distributed tracing
projects.summary: Switched two Python services to structured JSON logs with request IDs and added OpenTelemetry tracing exported to GCP.
projects.problem: Logs were plain text without request IDs, so following a single failing request across services was slow and manual.
objectives: Make every log line searchable by request ID.
Trace requests across the shipments API and notifications service.
my_contributions: Changed the existing logging setup to output structured JSON with a request ID on every line.
Added request ID middleware using contextvars and propagated the ID to outgoing calls.
Integrated OpenTelemetry tracing for FastAPI and HTTP clients, exporting to Cloud Trace.
Updated Dockerfiles and Cloud Run service settings for the new configuration.
projects.implementation: A FastAPI middleware reads or creates an X-Request-ID header and stores it in a contextvar. A logging filter adds it to every JSON log record. The OpenTelemetry SDK auto-instruments FastAPI, SQLAlchemy and httpx, with traces exported to Cloud Trace at a 10% sampling rate.

challenges.challenge: Full tracing and debug logging increased logging costs.
challenges.solution: Sampled 10% of traces and disabled debug logs in production through configuration.

decisions.context: Request IDs had to be available everywhere without passing them through every function.
decisions.decision: Store the request ID in a contextvar set by middleware.
decisions.reasoning: Works with async code and needs no changes to function signatures.
